prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "VISA INC." (ticker V), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "V", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Visa Inc.
markets: Commercial and money movement payments (B2B, Visa Direct)
Value-added services (risk, fraud, tokenization, data, issuing and acceptance tools)
Digital and agentic commerce credentials and stablecoin settlement

mission.statement: Our purpose is to uplift everyone, everywhere by being the best way to pay and be paid.
mission.source: Visa Inc. Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 (purpose statement)
mission.plain: Visa wants paying and getting paid to be easy and safe for every person and business in the world.

about.plain: Visa runs the giant computer network that moves money when someone pays with a Visa card or phone. When you tap your card at a shop, Visa checks the payment and passes the money from your bank to the shop's bank in seconds. Visa does not lend money or issue the cards itself; banks do that. Visa earns a small fee on every payment that runs over its network.
about.customers: Banks that hand out Visa cards, the banks and payment companies that serve shops, and businesses and governments that send money.
about.everyday: The Visa logo is on nearly 5 billion cards and on the payment screens of shops, websites and phones around the world.

money.plain: fees for checking, approving and settling each card payment (share of gross revenue before client incentives)
fees banks pay based on how much people spend on Visa cards
extra fees when a card is used in another country or currency
consulting, data, card benefits and licensing fees
fraud and risk tools, tokens, data and issuer software sold on top of the network
settling payments in stablecoins and letting AI assistants pay safely with Visa credentials

result.summary: Visa has one of the widest moats in business: a two-sided network that links nearly 5 billion credentials with well over 100 million merchant locations, so every new card makes acceptance more valuable and vice versa. Its scale lets it process 258 billion transactions a year at about a 60% operating margin. The main risks come from regulators and from government-backed real-time payment systems, not from a rival card network.

pricingPower.evidence: Net revenue rose from $21,846M in FY2020 to $40,000M in FY2025 while operating margin stayed near 60%, helped by periodic network-fee increases with no visible loss of volume; payments volume reached $17 trillion in FY2025 and nine-month FY2026 net revenue grew 15.3%. Limits are regulatory: the US DOJ debit antitrust suit (2024), interchange settlements with merchants and the proposed Credit Card Competition Act.

moats.evidence: Visa is consistently ranked among the world's most valuable brands, and its logo signals guaranteed acceptance and fraud protection to consumers in more than 200 countries and territories.

Issuers sign multi-year network agreements backed by large client incentives (Visa paid $15,751M of incentives in FY2025), and reissuing millions of cards and recoding systems makes switching costly, though big banks can and occasionally do move portfolios to Mastercard.

Nearly 5 billion Visa credentials and global merchant acceptance reinforce each other, and Visa says about 12 billion cards, accounts and wallets connect to its network; a new entrant would need both sides at once.
Visa processed 258 billion transactions in FY2025, spreading fixed technology costs so thinly that it earns about a 60% GAAP operating margin.
Global card networks form a duopoly outside China (Visa and Mastercard), because a market can only economically support a few universally accepted networks.
Visa's neutral, bank-partnered model (it takes no credit risk) is hard for lending networks like American Express to copy, but it is an incumbent rather than a disruptor.
Decades of fraud data feed AI risk tools such as Visa Advanced Authorization and tokenization, which Visa says prevent billions of dollars of fraud a year.
Visa has no exclusive asset beyond its network and brand; its VisaNet data centers could in principle be replicated.

customers.evidence: Visa's largest issuing clients renew multi-year network agreements, consumers rarely choose against Visa because acceptance is near universal, and payments volume reached $17 trillion in FY2025; merchants, by contrast, resent its fees.

talent.evidence: Visa's high margins fund competitive pay, employees grew from about 31,600 to 34,100 in FY2025, and it regularly appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies list.

product.evidence: VisaNet is among the most reliable and fastest payment networks in the world, and Visa led industry standards such as contactless (EMV), network tokenization and Visa Intelligent Commerce for AI-agent payments.

competitors.name: Mastercard Incorporated
competitors.note: The other global card network; competes for every issuer contract, merchant, cross-border flow and value-added service.

competitors.name: American Express Company
competitors.note: Closed-loop premium card network and issuer competing for high-spend consumer and corporate card volume.

competitors.name: Capital One Financial Corporation (Discover Global Network)
competitors.note: Bought Discover in 2025 and is moving its debit and some credit cards onto the Discover/Pulse networks, pulling volume off Visa.

competitors.name: China UnionPay
competitors.note: Largest card network by cards issued; dominant inside China and growing acceptance abroad.

competitors.name: PayPal Holdings, Inc.
competitors.note: Digital wallet and Venmo that can route payments through bank accounts instead of cards; also a big Visa partner.

competitors.name: National Payments Corporation of India (UPI)
competitors.note: Government-backed real-time payment system that handles most of India's digital payments, limiting card growth.

competitors.name: Banco Central do Brasil (Pix)
competitors.note: Free instant payment system in Brazil that has taken share from debit cards.

competitors.name: JCB Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Japanese card network competing mainly in Japan and Asian travel spending.

competitors.name: Block, Inc.
competitors.note: Cash App and Square encourage pay-by-bank and peer-to-peer flows that bypass card rails.

competitors.name: Apple Inc.
competitors.note: Apple Pay controls the digital wallet layer and could steer payments toward pay-by-bank options.

competitors.name: Stripe, Inc.
competitors.note: Payment processor building stablecoin (Bridge, Tempo) and bank-payment alternatives to card networks.

competitors.name: Adyen N.V.
competitors.note: Global payment processor that partners with card networks but pushes local and account-to-account methods.

estimates.name: Capital One Financial Corporation (Discover Global Network)

threats: US regulation: the DOJ's 2024 debit monopolization lawsuit, merchant interchange litigation and settlements, and the proposed Credit Card Competition Act that would force routing choice on credit cards.
Government-backed real-time payment systems such as UPI (India), Pix (Brazil) and FedNow (US) that make account-to-account payments free and instant.
Stablecoins and pay-by-bank checkout from Stripe, PayPal, Apple and others that could route online payments around card rails.
Capital One moving Discover-network debit and credit volume off Visa after its 2025 Discover acquisition.
Ongoing litigation costs: FY2025 operating expenses jumped to $16,006M from $12,331M partly because of litigation provisions.

ceo.name: Ryan McInerney
ceo.background: Finance graduate of the University of Notre Dame, former McKinsey principal and CEO of Chase consumer banking at JPMorgan Chase; joined Visa as president in 2013.

c1.evidence: Visa leads global digital payments, which still grow double digits as cash declines, but card networks are a maturing industry rather than an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Banks and merchants choose Visa for near-universal acceptance and reliability across nearly 5 billion credentials, a two-sided network effect that has lasted decades and is very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Visa is a household name and the default card network worldwide, the brand most cards in people's wallets carry.

c4.evidence: Visa repeats its purpose of uplifting everyone, everywhere by being the best way to pay and be paid, and pushes financial inclusion, but it is run as a highly profitable, shareholder-focused company.

c6.evidence: “everywhere, trusted, convenient”; the impression is mostly positive among consumers, though merchants complain about swipe fees.

c7.evidence: Visa's FY2025 10-K cites a roughly $520 billion annual value-added-services revenue opportunity on top of trillions of dollars of consumer and business payments still made in cash, checks and bank transfers, riding the secular shift to digital payments.

c8.evidence: Visa Direct, B2B payments, value-added services, stablecoin settlement and Visa Intelligent Commerce for AI-agent shopping all extend the network into large new markets.

m1.evidence: McInerney has articulated a network-of-networks strategy and early bets on agentic commerce and stablecoins, but his style is that of a disciplined operator rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: McInerney is a professional manager hired from JPMorgan, not a founder, though he has spent over a decade at Visa.

m4.evidence: He emphasises clients and partners in Visa's network strategy, but there is little public evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Visa keeps launching products such as tokenization, Visa Direct and Visa Intelligent Commerce, but its culture is corporate and cautious rather than founder-driven.

m6.evidence: McInerney has a finance and consulting background rather than an engineering one.

m7.evidence: No controversies attach to him personally, and Visa backs financial-inclusion and small-business programs, but its priorities are mostly commercial.

m7b.evidence: No record found of McInerney giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: McInerney keeps a low public profile and is not known for a distinctive public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2023, net revenue grew from $32,653M (FY2023) to $40,000M (FY2025), and nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 15.3%.

m10.evidence: Visa is known for cost discipline and high margins, but not for a culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: Visa's network handled $17 trillion of payments and cash volume in FY2025, letting billions of people pay safely almost anywhere in the world.

p2.evidence: Running a network that handles hundreds of billions of transactions a year with near-perfect uptime and real-time fraud scoring is extremely hard and is critical financial infrastructure.

f1.evidence: Net revenue rose every year from $21,846M in FY2020 to $40,000M in FY2025.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin slipped from 64.5% in FY2020 to 60.0% in FY2025, largely because of litigation provisions and higher spending.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt was $23,858M against $13,792M of cash and short-term investments and about $23B of yearly operating cash flow, with $35,178M of equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $14,081M (FY2020) to $23,994M (FY2025) and operating cash flow from $10,440M to $23,059M.

v1.evidence: Visa is the largest network, accepted almost everywhere, but for an ordinary person a Mastercard works nearly as well, so the edge over its main rival is small.

v2.evidence: Visa appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies list and pays well, but it is not usually among the top employers in rankings such as Glassdoor's Best Places to Work.

c5.evidence: If Visa vanished overnight billions of cardholders and millions of merchants would be unable to pay or be paid, causing chaos in shops, travel and online commerce worldwide.
